newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romanian forex market confused as curbs are removed.
newsitem.headline: Romanian forex market confused as curbs are removed.

text.p: The removal this week of curbs on Romania's foreign exchange market has plunged traders into confusion and left the leu currency struggling to find a level consistent with the country's economic progress.
The central bank (BNR) this week reissued dealer licences withdrawn from 24 banks last year when the former leftist government tried to keep the leu overvalued before elections it eventually lost.

For the past year only four banks have been allowed to act as market makers and impose rates. But since the restriction was lifted, the leu has tumbled 20 percent, continuing a plunge which began two months ago.
"We are as confused as we were a year ago when the market was restricted," said one trader. "There is still a long way to go before we can say our market is operating properly."

Operators were reluctant to forecast the behaviour of the leu, which has fallen this week to 9,000 to the dollar from about 4,000 in the New Year. Most said they were waiting for the central bank's next moves.
"I don't think anyone can realistically give a forecast for the leu's level," said a trader with a foreign bank.

Under the new centrist government's market reform package, the BNR has tightened monetary policy to fight inflation and restore confidence in the leu. Its drive pushed money market rates this week to about 290 percent from 52 in January.

Some traders said the BNR might press home its moves by compelling banks to hold all their minimum reserves in lei. Under present rules commercial banks can hold part of their reverves in hard currency.
Others said the BNR was poised to limit loans in hard currency which banks can extend to local businesses. These rose to $2.45 billion last year from $1.88 billion in 1995.
Central bank governor Mugur Isarescu says he hopes the leu will not fall faster than inflation, which he estimates at an year-on-year 89.5 percent, compared with last year's 56.9.
But he has declined to forecast a long-term level, saying only that the rate would be set strictly by the market, which would eventually eliminate current large gaps between dealers.
"It is a war of attrition but it will clearly subside," he said, adding that the BNR aimed to offer leu holders "substantial gains this year".
Some traders said that even though hard currency holders were keen to see the leu slide further, recent squeezes on the leu money market might force some to part with their dollars.

They said most banks short of lei might leave their minimum reserves below target and be hit with penalties at the punishing Lombard rate, which jumped to 362.16 percent from last week's 200.72 percent.

"With such a 'leu hunger', the leu may try to resist the mighty greenback and even gain some ground," said one trader. But he said inflationary fears could also undermine the leu's attempts to stabilise.
Monthly inflation soared to 13.7 percent in January from 10.3 percent in December. No letup is seen for months after the freeing of prices for fuel, electicity and food, introduced from this week.

With the government committed to cutting big budget and trade deficits, and speeding up structural reforms and privatisation, monthly inflation is forecast to slow to about 2.2 percent by the year-end.
Traders said a second innovation this week by the BNR, the abandoning of a leu "reference rate", a weighted average based on their daily reports, had no impact on the currency trend.
